reviewQuote: Eli Roth’s Ice Cream Man had the potential to be a fun, over-the-top B-horror movie, but it’s undone by flat performances, inconsistent tone, and a messy script. Easily one of the worst movies of the year!
I can’t defend it on most rational levels, but as a piece of exploitation fare, it recreates the vibe of the trash classics Roth was obviously inspired by.
As graphic and intense as writer/director Eli Roth's Hostel movies but applied to a good-naturedly macabre romp.

Much like the ice cream itself, the moments of outrageously grisly fun (following an unforgivably slow first act) in Ice Cream Man unfortunately and quickly dry up. My thoughts are also lowered learning AI was used
Ice Cream Man is Roth’s sickening idea of a good time, and I have to admit, I had a good time with it, too.

I am not, by any stretch of the imagination, a fan of horror films. I am a guy who loves movies, though, and can appreciate good filmmaking – even if it is a horror movie. I do not consider "Ice Cream Man" a good movie.
Most Eli Roth fans will turn on Ice Cream Man hoping for 90 minutes or so of excruciating brutal, inventive and gratuitous gore. And those fans won’t be disappointed.
This is a Roth original and it may be the most Eli Rothiest thing he has ever done. The kills are over the top and the story is unremarkable in its best moments and irritating at worst.
Awful dialogue, non-existent characterizations, an unremarkable villain, and obnoxious AI-generated images. As memorable and enjoyable as a post-dessert stomach ache.
It’s a badly made snow cone, where the cheap syrup hasn’t gotten through the ice: a flat, one dimensional, and mostly flavorless affair.
The latest from Eli Roth is terrible. (Insert tedious ice cream-related pun here.)
With Ice Cream Man, Roth has an interesting idea, but with so little behind it, the movie quickly melts.
An asinine, repetitive and unimaginative horror comedy that's neither funny, bonkers nor scary enough to become a guilty pleasure.
It’s mostly pretty satisfying, even if there’s ultimately nothing surprising or essential here.
Eli Roth's ode to old-school practical FX stumbles on genre basics.
Roth strips things back so aggressively that all that’s left is about 83 minutes of relentless bloodshed propping up the barest outline of a story.
A tedious and repetitive gorefest that never manages to feel scary or even tense, despite the shock value.
I wanted to believe Thanksgiving marked the beginning of a new chapter for Roth. Instead, Ice Cream Man feels less like the next step forward and more like a disappointing slide back into old habits.

weak performances, clunky dialogue, flat comedy, and surprisingly uninspired direction prevent the movie from capitalizing on any of its strengths. Even the title character ends up feeling like an afterthought.
If you know that you’re just in for a gorefest with a demented edge, you’re sure to have a good time, even if it lacks much in the way of cinematic nutritional value.
...just 10 minutes into this Eli Roth movie, I was not happy. It all feels too stiff, the editing is sloppy, and the plot is virtually non-existent. Yeah, I’m disappointed.
A relatively fun first 30 minutes that then goes on for another 60 minutes. Would have made a better fake trailer for Grindhouse 2 than a feature.
It’s a movie that inflicts plenty of head trauma but ultimately reveals itself as having no real brains of its own.
A convincingly assembled nightmare that horror fanatics will probably enjoy for its sheer gross-out factor. But as with most of Roth’s output, the problem lies in the screenplay.

It would be more exciting to watch a documentary about the professionals, weirdos and professional weirdos making the fake guts and disembodied limbs than to watch the film they were actually working on.

This creative zeal eventually sputters out. Thanksgiving used inventive variations on its gimmick to build toward its sicko smorgasbord finale, an escalation of gnarly ingenuity that Ice Cream Man lacks.

Ice Cream Man is depraved fun served exactly how it should be -- cold, messy, and with zero apologies. Eli Roth made the movie only he would dare to make, and horror fans with a strong stomach should line up for a scoop.

After a while, it becomes clear there are only so many grotesque Roth motifs that the human body lends itself to. But that doesn’t stop him from going on and on, again and again. Thankfully, the director has more than gore on his mind.
It’s like Roth forgot to put his film in the freezer, and all the decorative appeal, or any valuable substance, melted away.

There have been plenty of horror movies involving murderous children over the years... But Roth doesn’t hide his desire to outdo them all with this effort that can only be described as sick and twisted. And I’m sure he’ll take that as a compliment.

That the film knows it’s preposterous is supposed to be redeeming. But Roth’s it’s-all-a-big-joke attitude here is a cop-out that’s beneath him, a way to avoid making a horror movie that truly engages us.
Unfortunately the timing is off as this underdeveloped concept looks like a bad attempted imitation of last summer’s far superior Zach Cregger directed smash hit Oscar winning Weapons.
I give it two scoops down.
From the man known for some of the goriest films ever, this might be his bloodiest yet. A fun and violent over-the-top gorefest.

Eli Roth aims for social commentary in the homestretch, but if the moment doesn’t feel satisfyingly nihilistic, that’s because his stab at building out the story has all the consistency of soft serve.
Ice Cream Man is the perfect summer horror flick. It is fun, and it doesn’t have anything that is going to require thought or pondering your own trauma. It’s just gory goodness.

Suddenly, the lack of imagination in Ice Cream Man's execution doesn't seem so easily forgivable. Instead, it looks more and more like a wasted opportunity to make something interesting out of its fun idea.
"Ice Cream Man" intends to be splattery fun, but Roth can’t sustain momentum, going convoluted with his writing, and he tires out long before the feature concludes.
Eli Roth follows up his "Thanksgiving" with dessert, but the ice cream, while tasty at first, drops off its cone and splats to the ground when it gets to the stickiness of plot mechanics.
